metadata.title: What's an AI Inventory?
metadata.purpose: Answer what should come first when a legal team starts using AI tools ad hoc: a policy, or an inventory. Lands the carry-out that you can't govern a tool you haven't listed -- the inventory has to come before the policy.
metadata.source_note: Source sheet's narration carried unfilled '>' template placeholders at every skill-specific fact, and its named source_skill file does not exist on this machine -- see QUESTION.md. This redo reconstructs a generic, defensible AI-inventory account from the title/family rather than lifting facts that were never written.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B03 (the contract-review tool quietly adopted last spring: unlogged and invisible, then entered with the same four fields as everything else)

beats.narration_text: Someone on a legal team asks if they need an AI policy before rolling out a new tool. Wrong first word — you can't cover tools you haven't listed. Inventory first. Liam, take it from here.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Do we need an AI policy before we use this?', hesitates on 'policy', corrects to 'inventory', lands the real question

props.text:

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('policy' -> 'inventory') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: Here's the tempting move — write a policy tomorrow. Rules about which AI tools are allowed. Now look at what that actually does. A policy is a checklist against names; it governs the ones someone remembered to type in and nothing else. Anything adopted quietly slips past every time — the policy never knew it existed. They optimized policy for controlling known tools, at the expense of covering the unknown ones. What actually closes that gap isn't a tighter rule. It's a live list of what's already running.

shot.new_visual_element: A policy document card with a padlock, listing named tools; a fourth, unlabeled tool sliding in beneath it, unmarked and unlit

production_viz.label: A policy only governs what's named
production_viz.mechanic: A card labelled 'AI POLICY' with a padlock glyph and three named tool chips inside it, fully lit. A fourth chip slides in from below the card, dim and unlit, passing underneath without touching the policy card. A caption fades in beneath: 'the policy never knew it existed.'

beats.narration_text: An inventory is four fields per tool. What it does. What data touches it. Who owns it. A risk tier, set by how sensitive that data is. That's the whole shape. Same four questions every time — a missing field is visible in a glance, and comparison across tools is trivial. They optimized for uniform structure over expressive detail. Watch the anchor. The contract-review tool your litigation team quietly started using last spring — nobody wrote it into any policy, because nobody wrote it down anywhere.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- four field chips lighting in turn (what it does / data / owner / risk tier), then a dim, unlabeled tool card set off to the side

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- four fields, then the unlogged tool
production_viz.mechanic: Four chips fade in one at a time across the top, each labelled with a field (what it does / data touched / owner / risk tier), then fade out together. THE ANCHOR. A single card appears off to the side, dim and outlined only, reading 'contract-review tool' with no fields filled in -- visibly incomplete against the four-field shape just shown. THIS EXACT CARD RETURNS, FILLED IN, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: Enter that contract-review tool into the four fields — what, data, owner, risk — and it stops running unnoticed. Now watch what the inventory doesn't do. The risk tier isn't a verdict, it's a flag that says look at this; high-risk means surfaced, not cleared. And the list isn't a monument — the tool your team adopts tomorrow needs the same four fields before the list can call itself current. Here's the trade-off: they optimized inventory for visibility, not judgment. It shows you what to look at. What to do about it is still on you.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- the dim card lighting up with all four fields filled and sliding into the main list; then split into 'logged is not safe' and 'complete is not permanent'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- logged, not cleared
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 DIM CARD RETURNS, identical placement, and fills in one field at a time (what it does / data touched / owner / risk tier) until fully lit, then slides into a row alongside other completed entries. It splits into two cards: left reads 'risk tier: flag for review' with a struck-through 'SAFE' beneath it labelled 'logged is not safe'; right reads 'list: complete today' with a faint new unlabeled card appearing at its edge labelled 'complete is not permanent'.

beats.narration_text: You can't govern an AI tool you haven't listed. Build the inventory before you write the policy — the policy only works once you know what it has to cover.

props.quote: You can't govern an AI tool you haven't listed. Build the inventory before you write the policy — the policy only works once you know what it has to cover.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I'm on a legal team and I want a first-pass AI inventory. List every AI tool a small legal team might have adopted in the last year — drafting help, contract review, research search, transcription, anything. For each one, give me four fields: what it does, what data goes through it, who owns it, and a risk tier based on data sensitivity. Then flag the two most likely to have slipped in unlogged. Go deeper: take the highest-risk entry and tell me exactly what to ask the owner before that tool touches another client file.
